title: Superfund

definition.text: The common name for the 1980 US law (CERCLA) and its trust fund that pay for cleaning up abandoned hazardous waste sites and make polluters liable for the costs.

facts.text: Congress passed it in 1980 in response to hazardous waste disasters such as Love Canal in New York.
Because responsible parties were hard to find, it set up a fund financed by taxes on certain industries plus a broad liability framework.
Liability is generally joint and several: each potentially responsible party can be held liable for the whole cleanup cost, then seek contributions from others.
Historically about 70 percent of Superfund cleanups have been paid for by potentially responsible parties.
Until the mid-1990s an excise tax on the petroleum and chemical industries funded it, reflecting polluter pays; after it lapsed, taxpayers bore most costs until a chemical tax returned in 2021.
Sites are scored from 0 to 100 by a Hazard Ranking System; a score of 28.5 puts a site on the National Priorities List for long-term cleanup.
Its strict, no-fault liability has been blamed for creating brownfields, as investors avoid contaminated land for greenfield sites.
Minority and low-income communities have had less chance of getting nearby sites listed and cleaned up than richer areas.

notes: US programme kept as the course's main example of liability-based cleanup and polluter-pays funding; 12 in-scope inlinks.

title: Zoning

definition.text: A way for a local government to divide land into zones, each with its own rules on what may be built and how the land may be used.

facts.text: Zones may allow a single use such as housing or industry, mix compatible uses, or, in form-based zoning, govern building size and shape whatever the use.
Single-use zoning separates uses thought incompatible; in practice it also protects existing uses and a community's character.
Overlay zones add rules for a particular concern such as wetlands or a natural hazard without rewriting the whole code.
Environmental activists argue that separating everyday uses forces car ownership and increases traffic.
Some economists say zoning reduces efficiency and raises housing costs; one 2017 study estimated large GDP gains from partial deregulation.
Zoning regulations and land-use measures are key institutional tools for climate change adaptation and flood management in cities.

contested_note: Critics argue zoning raises housing costs, inequality and car dependence, while supporters see it as essential to separate harmful uses.

definition.text: Flexible zoning approaches that judge projects by their effects or let developers build more in return for public benefits such as open space.

facts.text: Performance zoning, first advocated by Lane Kendig in 1973, may let developers earn points for limiting environmental impacts or adding public amenities.
US cities most often use incentive zoning to win mixed use, open space conservation, walkability, affordable housing and parks.
Cluster zoning lets homes sit closer together so more land is kept as open space.
